query: Consider noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles containing more than five elements and targeted in a single-phase solid-solution state. Their crystal structure is difficult to control at fixed composition, while unsuccessful formation can involve phase separation, elemental segregation, uncontrolled particle morphology, and high thermal decomposition temperatures under synthesis regimes with rapid heating and cooling. What testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs formation and crystal-structure selection in this regime and why? Define a controlled intervention without specifying a technique, predict the observations relative to the initial single-phase baseline, identify the applicable compositional and processing boundaries, cite supporting evidence, and state a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Formation and crystal‐structure selection in noble‐metal high‐entropy alloy nanoparticles under rapid thermal processing is governed by a critical processing temperature threshold at which atomic diffusion rates overcome surface‐energy–driven nucleation barriers. Above this threshold, homogeneous fcc solid‐solution nuclei grow beyond the critical size, yielding single‐phase nanoparticles; below it, diffusion is insufficient, resulting in phase separation, elemental segregation, and irregular morphology.
generation.material_initial_state: Equimolar 5-element noble-metal HEA nanoparticles synthesized by a rapid heating/cooling regime that yields a single‐phase fcc solid solution (particle diameter ≈5 nm, confirmed by sharp XRD fcc peaks and uniform TEM-EDS elemental maps).
generation.intervention: Systematic variation of the maximum processing temperature (Tmax) during the rapid heating ramp, while holding composition, heating/cooling rates, dwell time, and atmosphere constant.
generation.conditions: Composition: equimolar Ir–Pt–Pd–Au–Rh; Tmax varied from 500 °C to 1000 °C; heating/cooling rates ≈10^5 K/s; dwell time ≈1 s; inert Ar atmosphere.
generation.structural_mediator: Critical nucleus size determined by the balance of element‐specific surface energies (which set the nucleation barrier) and temperature‐dependent atomic diffusivities.
generation.mechanism: Above a threshold Tmax (~800 °C), increased diffusivity enables individual element atoms to overcome surface‐energy barriers and co‐nucleate into a homogeneous fcc phase; below the threshold, limited atomic mobility leads to sub‐critical nuclei that separate by element and yield mixed or segregated phases with irregular shapes.
generation.predicted_outcome: For Tmax ≥ threshold, XRD will show single‐phase fcc peaks with narrow full‐width at half‐maximum (FWHM) and TEM-EDS maps will be uniform; for Tmax < threshold, XRD will display multiple or broadened peaks, TEM-EDS will reveal elemental segregation regions ≥20 % of particle volume, and particles will be irregular.
generation.baseline: Single‐phase fcc HEA nanoparticles form when Tmax ≈1000 °C under the given rapid thermal regime.
generation.boundary: Equimolar 5-element noble‐metal HEAs (Ir, Pt, Pd, Au, Rh); Tmax 500–1000 °C; heating/cooling rates ≈10^5 K/s; dwell time ≈1 s; inert Ar.
generation.uncertainty: The exact threshold temperature may vary by ±50 °C due to multicomponent diffusion coefficient uncertainties; surface energies in 5-element systems are not precisely known.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize equimolar Ir–Pt–Pd–Au–Rh HEA nanoparticles across Tmax = 500–1000 °C (fixed rates, dwell, atmosphere) and characterize phase, elemental distribution, and morphology.
measurements: X-ray diffraction phase identification and peak‐width analysis
Particle size and shape distribution by TEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If all samples—across the full Tmax range—exhibit the same single‐phase fcc structure, uniform elemental distribution, and similar morphology (no systematic change with Tmax), the hypothesis is falsified.
